title: Active recall: pull it out of your head
hook: Why pulling an answer out of memory beats reading it again, and how every lesson here uses it.

steps.prompt: Which formula was NOT on the list?
steps.why: That little strain of digging it back out is the point. Retrieving is what makes a memory stronger.

steps.prompt: Without scrolling back: write down as many of the five formulas as you can.
steps.answer: Slope, circle, percent change, triangle area and the Pythagorean theorem. Whatever you missed is what to practice.

steps.prompt: Before we start, from memory: which works better for remembering, rereading your notes or testing yourself?
steps.answer: Testing yourself. Pulling an answer out of memory (retrieval) strengthens it far more than reading it again.

steps.prompt: Ana and Ben study the same page for 20 minutes. Ana rereads it four times. Ben reads it once, then writes down everything he remembers and checks it. A week later, who remembers more?
steps.why: Retrieval practice beats rereading in study after study. Ben's effort to pull the ideas back out is what made them stick.

steps.prompt: Why does rereading feel like it's working?
choices: The words look familiar, so it feels like knowing them
Your brain stores more each time you read
Reading is the most active kind of study
steps.why: Familiar isn't the same as recallable. On test day you have to produce the answer, not recognize the page.

steps.prompt: Put the active recall loop in order.
items: Write or say everything you can remember
Check against the notes and mark what you missed
Start with the misses next time
steps.why: Try first, check second, and spend your next session on what you missed.

steps.prompt: Maya's plan for learning the slope formula. Tap the step that breaks active recall.
lines: Read the slope formula and one example
Cover it and write the formula from memory
Keep the answer key open while solving the next five problems
Check her work and redo the ones she missed
steps.why: Peeking turns recall back into recognition. Try each problem first, then check.

steps.prompt: You try to recall the quadratic formula and get stuck halfway. What's the best move?
choices: Keep trying for a moment, then check, then try it again later today
Skip it, since it might not be on the test
steps.why: A little struggle before checking is part of what makes it stick. Then retrieve it again later, from scratch.

steps.prompt: Which kind of step in these lessons is active recall?
steps.why: Every step makes you produce an answer before you see one. That's the whole design.

keys: Testing yourself beats rereading: pulling it out is what makes it stick.
Familiar isn't the same as remembered. Check yourself by producing the answer.
Try first, check second, and come back to your misses.

choices: Writing what you remember, then checking
recall.why: Retrieval, not review, is what strengthens memory.

choices: It makes the material feel familiar
It uses the wrong part of the brain
recall.why: Familiarity feels like knowing, but the test asks you to produce the answer.

recall.prompt: You can't remember a formula. Best first move?
choices: Try for a moment, then check
recall.why: A short effort to retrieve, then a check, makes the next recall easier.
